papers.title: Single-cell transcriptomic analysis reveals autophagy-associated transcriptional vulnerability of dopaminergic neurons after atrazine exposure.
papers.summary: This study uses single-cell RNA sequencing to examine how the herbicide atrazine affects dopaminergic neurons in the brain. The researchers found that atrazine exposure alters the expression of genes involved in autophagy, suggesting these neurons become transcriptionally vulnerable under toxic stress. This points to a link between environmental chemical exposure, autophagy dysregulation, and dopaminergic neuron susceptibility, relevant to conditions like Parkinson's disease.
papers.why: This paper's identification of autophagy-associated transcriptional vulnerability in dopaminergic neurons provides single-cell resolution insight into autophagy gene dysregulation that could inform how mitophagy/autophagy pathways are mapped onto neuronal subtypes in spatial transcriptomic studies.

papers.title: The research Progress on microtubules and Mitophagy-related diseases.
papers.summary: This paper reviews current knowledge on how microtubules interact with mitophagy, the process cells use to remove damaged mitochondria. It likely covers how microtubule dynamics and motor proteins help transport damaged mitochondria to sites of degradation, and how disruptions in this system are linked to various diseases. As a review, it probably synthesizes findings across neurodegenerative and other disease contexts without presenting new experimental data.
papers.why: Understanding how microtubule-dependent transport underlies mitophagy provides mechanistic context relevant to neuronal mitophagy dysfunction, which is central to this PhD project's focus on mitophagy in brain neurons.

papers.title: Zinc activates autophagy by regulating HDAC6 expression following cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury.
papers.summary: This study investigates how zinc influences autophagy after cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury, a common model for stroke-related brain damage. The researchers focus on HDAC6, an enzyme known to regulate protein and organelle degradation pathways, as a molecular link between zinc signaling and autophagy activation. The findings suggest zinc modulates HDAC6 expression to control autophagic responses in the injured brain.
papers.why: Since HDAC6-mediated autophagy regulation is mechanistically related to mitophagy pathways in neurons, this paper could offer insight into molecular regulators relevant to the PhD project's focus on neuronal autophagy, even though it doesn't directly address spatial transcriptomics, perineuronal nets, or interneurons.

papers.title: Dibucaine induces autophagic flux and reduces Ser129-phosphorylated <i>α</i>-synuclein in induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neurons with <i>SNCA</i> duplication.
papers.summary: This study tests dibucaine, a local anesthetic compound, on neurons derived from induced pluripotent stem cells carrying a duplication of the SNCA gene, which causes familial Parkinson's disease. The researchers found that dibucaine boosts autophagic flux, meaning it enhances the cell's ability to clear damaged proteins and organelles through the autophagy pathway. As a result of this enhanced autophagy, the neurons showed reduced levels of a toxic, disease-associated form of α-synuclein (phosphorylated at Ser129), suggesting dibucaine could help clear harmful protein aggregates.
papers.why: This paper is relevant because it demonstrates a pharmacological approach to enhancing autophagic clearance of toxic protein aggregates in neurons, directly relevant to mitophagy/autophagy mechanisms being studied in the brain, even though the model system (iPSC-derived neurons, Parkinson's-related) differs from the primary focus on interneurons and perineuronal nets.

papers.title: GRP75-dependent SIMPA mediates inter-organellar quality control.
papers.summary: This paper describes a process called SIMPA, which depends on a protein called GRP75, that allows cells to coordinate quality control between different organelles. GRP75 is known to help connect mitochondria with other compartments like the endoplasmic reticulum, suggesting SIMPA may serve as a mechanism to clear or manage damaged organellar components across these contact sites. The study likely demonstrates how this inter-organellar communication helps maintain cellular health by targeting dysfunctional material for degradation.
papers.why: Understanding GRP75-mediated inter-organellar quality control is relevant to the profile's focus on mitophagy and autophagy mechanisms in neurons, since mitochondria-ER contact sites and related clearance pathways are central to how neurons manage organelle damage and could inform spatial analyses of mitophagy in brain tissue.

papers.title: USP4-Mediated Deubiquitination of PTBP1 Promotes Glioma Progression and Radioresistance by Enhancing PHB2-Dependent Mitophagy.
papers.summary: This study finds that an enzyme called USP4 removes a molecular tag (ubiquitin) from a protein called PTBP1, preventing PTBP1 from being degraded. Stabilized PTBP1 then boosts the activity of PHB2, a protein that drives mitophagy (the selective clearance of damaged mitochondria) in glioma cells. This enhanced mitophagy helps glioma tumors grow faster and resist radiation therapy.
papers.why: While focused on cancer rather than neurons, this paper offers mechanistic insight into PHB2-dependent mitophagy regulation that could inform how similar ubiquitination-based control of mitophagy operates in neuronal health and disease.

papers.title: Regulation of developmental autophagy at the nuclear periphery.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how autophagy, the cellular process of self-degradation and recycling, is regulated specifically at the nuclear periphery during development. It likely explores molecular machinery and signaling that localizes autophagic activity near the nuclear envelope, possibly involving nuclear pore complexes or lamina components. The findings presumably reveal a developmental stage-specific or tissue-specific mechanism controlling autophagy initiation or cargo selection near the nucleus.
papers.why: Understanding nuclear periphery-associated autophagy regulation could inform how mitophagy and autophagy pathways in neurons are spatially controlled within the cell, relevant to interneuron health and dysfunction.

papers.title: Dental Pulp Stem Cell-Derived Small Extracellular Vesicle miR-100-5p Attenuates Neuronal Oxidative Stress via Regulating the mTOR-Autophagy Signaling Axis.
papers.summary: This study looks at tiny vesicles released by dental pulp stem cells that carry a specific microRNA called miR-100-5p. The researchers found that these vesicles can be delivered to neurons and help protect them from oxidative stress damage. The protective effect works by influencing the mTOR signaling pathway, which in turn regulates autophagy activity in the neurons.
papers.why: This paper is relevant because it demonstrates a mTOR-autophagy signaling mechanism that protects neurons from oxidative stress, directly connecting to the project's focus on autophagy regulation in neurons.
